# The canal that made New York

When the Erie Canal opened in 1825, it cut the cost of shipping a ton of flour from Buffalo to New York City from roughly one hundred dollars to about ten. DeWitt Clinton, who had staked his political career on the project, was mocked for years as the builder of a ditch.

The mockery did not last. Within a decade, towns such as Rochester and Syracuse grew from villages into cities, and the port of New York overtook Philadelphia and Boston as the nation's busiest. Farmers in Ohio who had once hauled grain over the Appalachians by wagon could now reach the Atlantic in a matter of weeks.

The canal's success was never only about engineering. It was about a state willing to borrow against an uncertain future, and about the Irish and local laborers who dug most of its 363 miles by hand.
